name: Hydrafacial

card.summary: A branded in-clinic cleansing and exfoliating facial that uses suction and serums; popular and low-downtime, with only a small published evidence base.
card.note: Cosmetic maintenance treatment; published studies are few, small and often manufacturer-linked.

quick.overview:
Hydrafacial is a branded, multi-step facial given by aestheticians or clinicians. It cleanses and exfoliates the skin, uses suction to clear pores, and then applies serums. It is a type of hydradermabrasion, which is itself classed as a variant of microdermabrasion.

It is discussed in skincare and appearance communities as a low-downtime option for a temporary glow and smoother texture. Published research is limited to a few small studies, including a 20-person open-label acne study and an imaging study of skin changes.
quick.mechanism: A handheld tip delivers a water-based solution and exfoliating agents to the skin while applying suction, removing dead surface cells and debris, followed by serums. The effect is superficial exfoliation rather than deep remodelling.
quick.risks: General microdermabrasion-type procedures are described as having few side effects, with temporary dryness, sun sensitivity or rare bruising reported. Results are temporary, so sessions are repeated. Costs vary by clinic.

lead: Hydrafacial is a branded facial treatment that combines cleansing, chemical exfoliation, suction-based extraction and serum application using a single handheld device. It is commonly described as a form of hydradermabrasion, which encyclopedias class as a type of microdermabrasion using water-based sprays and a textured tip [3].

It is offered in aesthetic clinics and spas and is discussed online as a maintenance treatment for a short-term glow and smoother skin, often before events. Published studies are few: an imaging study of eight volunteers used line-field confocal optical coherence tomography to examine microscopic skin changes [1], and an open-label trial in mild-to-moderate acne enrolled 20 adults, with investigator-rated clear or almost clear skin rising from 20 to 65 percent [2].

paras: The treatment is delivered in stages: cleansing and peeling, suction-based extraction, and infusion of serums. The acne study describes a three-step process of this kind [2]. Hydradermabrasion is classed as a type of microdermabrasion, a non-invasive exfoliation that removes the outermost dead cells and is typically repeated every few weeks [3].

The device is a single handheld unit with interchangeable tips that applies solutions and suction in the same pass. The acne protocol studied added a final step of blue LED light [2]. A scalp variant, HydraScalp or Keravive, applies a similar approach to the scalp and has been the subject of registered trials [5][6].

A 2024 study used line-field confocal optical coherence tomography, a non-invasive imaging method, to visualise microscopic changes in eight volunteers (Fitzpatrick skin types II-V) before treatment, after treatment and at two weeks. Average stratum corneum thickness fell from 9.42 to 6.67 micrometres immediately after treatment and was 9.75 micrometres at two weeks. The images also showed more homogeneous stratum corneum and fewer undulations in the epidermis. The superficial dermis appeared stretched after treatment and returned to baseline by two weeks, with no visible difference in dermal collagen fibres at follow-up. The authors say clinical studies validating the procedure with objective histological assessment have been scarce [1].

A 12-week multicenter open-label study enrolled 20 adults with mild-to-moderate acne at two US sites to receive six Clarifying Treatments, one every two weeks. The proportion with no acne or almost clear skin (Global Acne Severity Score of 1 or less) rose from 20 to 65 percent by investigator assessment and from 5 to 55 percent by patient report. More than 80 to 100 percent of investigators and patients agreed that skin appearance had improved across several parameters, and treatments were generally well tolerated. The authors note that blinding was not feasible and there was no control group [2].

Registered trials include a phase 4 study of three treatments on skin quality, hydration and barrier in 27 adults [4], and scalp studies of the Keravive variant in androgenetic alopecia (44 participants) [5] and self-perceived hair thinning (15 participants, not yet recruiting) [6].

sections.h: How it compares with other facials
paras: Wikipedia lists hydrafacials among types of facial alongside European facials, LED light therapy facials and mini-facials; facials as a family include steam, exfoliation, extraction, masks, peels and massage [7]. Dermabrasion-type treatments exfoliate the outermost dead cells and are typically repeated every few weeks [3].

Microdermabrasion in general is described as having few side effects, with temporary dryness, sun sensitivity or, rarely, bruising and scratches reported. Crystal-based systems carry additional risks such as eye injury, which do not apply to water-based designs [3].

Hydrafacial appears in skincare discussions as a convenient pre-event or maintenance treatment with little downtime. Users commonly describe it as a complement to daily skincare and, for acne, to medical treatment, since results are described as temporary [1][2].

angle.text: Hydrafacial is used for a short-term glow and smoother-looking skin, and in a published open-label study the clarifying version was used on acne-prone skin. Because the treatment is exfoliative, results are described as temporary and sessions are repeated.
